data.title: Šútovo/Ratkovo – a Púchov culture hillfort above the Váh
data.excerpt: A hillfort of the Púchov culture crowns a hill on the boundary of the cadastral areas of Ratkovo and Šútovo, at a narrowing of the Váh valley above the Krpeľany reservoir. The fortified settlement of some 0.19 ha controlled the meeting point of Liptov, Turiec and Orava, and the brooches found there show that it also served as a trade centre.

children.text: The hillfort of the Púchov culture, rising on a hill on the boundary of the cadastral areas of the villages of Ratkovo and Šútovo, is situated at an important strategic point beside the main communication route running along the right bank of the Váh in the area of the Krpeľany reservoir. It lies at a point where the valley of the Váh narrows and has the potential to control the surrounding space well. At the same time the hillfort forms a boundary point between Liptov and Turiec, and to a certain extent also Orava.

The shape of the fortified settlement, with an area of about 0.19 ha, is defined by the roughly kidney-shaped plan of the summit of the hill at the spot height of 557 m above sea level, oriented with its longer axis NNE–SSW. On the northern to north-eastern and the southern to south-eastern perimeter of the summit, traces of a rampart spread by erosion can be identified beyond doubt. The eastern side was not artificially modified, because, given the configuration of the terrain (a steep slope below the summit of the hill), the creation of a rampart was not necessary in these places for the purposes of securing the defence. The presence of a lighter form of fortification in the shape of a wooden palisade may, however, be assumed. The presence of an artificial fortification is likewise an open question on the western perimeter, which is defined by a pronounced ridge of natural origin, divided in the middle, below which, as on the eastern side, the ground falls away steeply. Access to the enclosure was provided by a gateway on the north-western side, placed between the rampart on the northern to north-eastern side and the natural ridge on the western edge of the summit. It is of interest that pits can also be found on the hillfort, most of which probably served as firing positions during the Second World War. This is indicated by the quantity of cartridge cases from the 1930s to the first half of the 1940s of the last century, which in several cases were concentrated precisely in the pits, or in their immediate vicinity.

The site was discovered in 1955 by A. Petrovský-Šichman and we class it among the smaller fortified settlements (the so-called hrádky, fortlets) of the La Tène period to the Early Roman period. In 2003 the hillfort was investigated by Robert Májsky, from whose article we have drawn. The pictures of the finds likewise come from this article.

The chronologically most important metal finds from the Hradisko site are four examples of brooches that can be assigned to the La Tène period, and an iron brooch of the Gebhard group. Further, an iron brooch with a Middle La Tène construction of the Kostrzewski variant, two iron brooches with a Late La Tène construction and a spoon-shaped head, and an iron pin with a four-coil spring and an internal chord were found. A socketed chisel, a small awl and a larger awl/graver served for working wood. Among the weapons, part of a spearhead was found.

A relatively marked concentration of pottery within the small area of the trench that was dug, together with the presence of burnt sandstones, suggests that this may have been part of a settlement feature that had been encountered. The chronologically most distinctive pieces are fragments of a characteristic jug of local Púchov provenance and the upper part of a situla with a narrow, sickle-shaped rim. In addition, the presence of several further fragments of typical pottery was established, distinguished by a more archaic character. This is a fragment of the neck of a jug pointing unambiguously still to pottery of the pre-Púchov stage, which, however, will evidently be contemporary with the rest of the pottery from the trench, and thus represents merely an older reminiscence within the Púchov milieu itself.

From the chronological point of view it is therefore possible to delimit the occupation of the hillfort by the people of the Púchov culture from the course of the later part of phase LT C2 to the later stage of phase LT D1 (LT D1b). Finds that would document its further continuation in phase LT D2, or even into the beginning of the Early Roman period – that is, finds that are exclusive indicators of these stages – are absent.

From the functional point of view, in the context of its position in the landscape and the character of the finds, the fortification can be seen above all as a strategic point serving to control an important route at the meeting place of two regions (Turiec and Liptov) and, to a certain extent indirectly, of a third as well (Orava). The site quite evidently also served as a trade centre, since part of the metal inventory – specifically the brooches – is foreign to the more central areas of the Púchov culture. In the case of the brooch of the Gebhard group, a direct import from the area of southern Germany may also be considered, though it is not out of the question that the example comes from western Slovakia, where several brooches of the Gebhard group in general (leaving aside the distinction of variants) were found at the hillfort of Molpír near Smolenice, and further ones are probable. This important Celtic centre may have played a part in their distribution further to the north, if indeed they were not produced here directly after western models. In the area of the Púchov culture an iron brooch of the Gebhard group 17 occurred at the hillfort of Požaha in Moravia, and the variant 17a apparently comes directly from Bošáca – their distribution likewise points to a western origin.

Apart from the functions set out above, however, it is also necessary to reckon with ordinary economic settlement activities of a productive character, as the iron tools and the spindle whorl recovered also indicate. Strategic functions need not, after all, be in any way incompatible with the role of a permanently occupied space with domestic or even specialised craft production. In any case, by the character of the occupation and the composition of the finds, the fortification does not correspond to the original general notion of the Púchov hrádky as places without permanent occupation, founded in the overwhelming majority only in the Late La Tène period and used more intensively only at the beginning of the Roman period. This conclusion will evidently have to be corrected, at least to a certain extent, in the case of other smaller fortifications as well, as some more recently recovered finds from further similar sites also suggest.
